title: API design
summary: An API is a contract that outlives its implementation: once clients depend on a path, a field or a status code, changing it costs every one of them a release. This lesson models the domain as resources with standard methods, uses HTTP's safe and idempotent semantics and status codes as the protocol defines them, settles one error shape, paginates every list from the first release, handles work that outlives the request with 202 and an operation resource, states what counts as a breaking change and how to version, writes the contract in OpenAPI or protobuf, and chooses REST, gRPC or GraphQL per boundary with a decision table.

blocks.text: Stripe versions its API by release date and pins each account to the version current at its first request, so no integration receives a breaking change until its owner upgrades; a Stripe-Version header overrides the pin per request. Each incompatible change is a version change module that transforms responses backwards from the current shape, which keeps old versions out of the core code and generates the changelog, and every outgoing change goes through a lightweight review on a mailing list before release.

Google publishes its API design rules as numbered API Improvement Proposals and enforces them with an API linter. The pagination proposal requires page_size and page_token on every list method from the first release, opaque tokens, and coercion rather than an error for an oversized page; the compatibility proposal forbids removing, renaming or retyping any component within a major version and treats a change of default behaviour as breaking.

Zalando's guidelines, which its teams must follow for every API, require pagination on every list, prefer cursors over offsets and discourage total counts; require Problem JSON for every error and forbid stack traces; and treat versioning as a last resort, with media type versioning when it cannot be avoided and URL versions banned. Shutting an API down requires the consent of every client on a sunset date and monitoring of the deprecated version's usage until then.

Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center guidance, used for the Azure REST APIs, returns 202 with the status endpoint in Location for any operation that would otherwise make the client wait, redirects with 303 to the created resource when the operation finishes, and documents four versioning mechanisms with the trade-off that a version in the URI leaks into every link.

The GraphQL project documents the N+1 problem and batching with DataLoader as the standard answer, and names demand control (paginated lists, depth and breadth limits, complexity analysis) as the server's protection against the queries its own flexibility invites.

subtopics.title: Resources, collections and the standard methods

blocks.text: An API is a contract that outlives the code behind it. Once clients depend on a field, a path or a status code, changing it costs every one of them a release, so the design work is in getting the shape right before the first client ships. Google's resource-oriented design, the pattern behind its public APIs, starts from one idea: the building blocks of an API are individually named resources, the nouns of the domain, and the relationships and hierarchy between them. A small set of standard methods supplies the verbs for most operations, and custom methods exist for the actions that the standard ones cannot express.

The Azure guidance gives the same rule from the HTTP side. Name resources with plural nouns and let the method carry the verb: a client creates an order with a POST to the orders collection, not with a call to a create-order path. Organise collections by ownership (the orders of a customer live under that customer) but keep the nesting shallow, because a path deeper than collection, item, collection becomes rigid. Two anti-patterns recur. A chatty API exposes many small resources, so a client needs several round trips to assemble one screen; and an API that mirrors the database tables leaks the storage model, so a schema change becomes an API change.

blocks.text: The standard methods matter because their semantics are consistent: a generated client, a gateway or a cache can treat every Get the same way without reading the documentation. Google's guidance therefore says to prefer them whenever the operation genuinely fits, and not to contort an action such as cancelling an order into an update of a status field. The custom method keeps the vocabulary honest: a client that calls cancel is stating its intent, and the server can refuse it with a precise error.
Write the resource list, the hierarchy and the schema of each resource before any path or method. The methods follow from the resources; the paths follow from the methods.

subtopics.title: Safe, idempotent and the status codes

blocks.text: HTTP's method properties are not style; intermediaries and client libraries act on them. RFC 9110 defines a method as safe when its semantics are essentially read-only, so the client requests no state change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. A method is idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests equals the effect of one: PUT, DELETE and the safe methods. POST is neither. The distinction exists so that automated retrieval and cache prefetching can use safe methods freely, and so that a client whose connection dropped before the response can repeat an idempotent request automatically.

The last point is the one that shapes API design. The RFC says a client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it has some means to know the semantics are idempotent, or to detect that the original was never applied. A POST that creates an order is exactly that case: a timeout leaves the client unable to tell whether the order exists. The fix is to make the operation idempotent by design with a client-supplied key, which the idempotency lesson covers; the API design decision is that every mutating endpoint states whether a repeat is safe and how.

blocks.caption: Status codes a client has to tell apart, and what each one means in RFC 9110.

accepted for processing, not completed; deliberately noncommittal
a long-running operation, with a link to its status
Delete, or an update with no body
the server will not process the request as sent
a malformed request; the error body says which field

an If-Match that did not match: another writer got there first

blocks.text: Two headers carry the rest of the story. Retry-After, sent with a 503 or a redirect, tells the client how long to wait as a date or a number of seconds, and it is the only standard way for an API to say when to come back. Conditional headers turn a read-modify-write into a safe update: the client sends If-Match with the version it read, and a 412 tells it another writer got there first. Zalando's guidelines add the throttling case: a caller over its limit gets a 429 with the rate-limit headers, never a generic client error.

A client that retries a POST on timeout, with no idempotency key, will create duplicates under exactly the conditions the retry was meant to survive. The RFC says not to; the API has to give the client a way to do it safely.

subtopics.title: One error shape for the whole API

blocks.text: An error response has three readers: the code that decides whether to retry, fix the request or give up; the developer reading a log; and the person who wrote the client, who sees the message in a support ticket a year later. The status code serves the first reader only partly, because a 400 does not say which field was wrong and a 409 does not say which state was in the way. RFC 9457 defines the standard answer, Problem Details, as a JSON object with the media type application/problem+json and five members.

blocks.caption: The members of a Problem Details object (RFC 9457). Any API may add extension members, such as a list of invalid fields.
rows: a URI that identifies the problem type
the machine-readable key; about:blank means the status code says it all
a short human-readable summary of the type
the same for every occurrence of that type
a copy for consumers that lost the status line
a human-readable explanation of this occurrence
written for the developer, never parsed by code
a URI for this specific occurrence
a correlation id or a request id in practice

blocks.text: Zalando's guidelines make the format mandatory for every error (MUST support problem JSON) and forbid exposing stack traces, because an internal class name or a SQL fragment in a response is both a leak and a dependency that some client will start parsing. The design principle underneath both rules is that anything a client needs to branch on is a stable, documented value in a named member, and anything written for a human may change at any time.

Validation errors are the common case and deserve a defined extension: a list of fields, each with the field path, a stable reason code and a message. A retryable condition should be distinguishable from a permanent one without parsing text, which is why the type URI and the status code together have to carry it: a 503 or a 429 with Retry-After is retryable, a 400 or a 409 is not. Document the whole shape once in the contract, under the components section, and reference it from every operation.

blocks.caption: A validation error as a Problem Details object with an errors extension member.

blocks.text: Every list method is paginated from its first release, and Google's pagination guidance explains why with an example. A user whose collection holds 75 resources deploys code that reads the whole list. The API later adds pagination with a default page of 50, and that code silently sees 50 and stops. Even a higher default only delays the break until the collection grows, and client libraries generate different method signatures for paginated calls, so adding pagination later is a backwards-incompatible change however it is done.

The Google shape is a page_size request field and a page_token field, both optional, with a next_page_token in the response that is empty only at the end of the collection. A page size above the maximum is coerced down, not rejected; a negative one is an error; the server may return fewer items than asked for even before the end. Tokens are opaque and URL-safe, and base64 over a readable value is not opacity: if users can decode a token they will, and the pagination internals become part of the API surface. A token carries position only, never authorisation, and may expire after a few days.

blocks.text: Filtering and sorting live in query parameters and are restricted to fields the store can serve from an index, since an open filter language is a way to run arbitrary scans. Partial responses let a client name the fields it wants, which keeps mobile payloads small, and a field mask on update names exactly the fields that change, which is the mechanism behind PATCH. The parameter names and behaviour are the same on every collection, so a client learns the conventions once.
Cap the page size on the server and document the default. The Azure guidance suggests either clamping an oversized request to the maximum or rejecting it; pick one and state it in the contract.

Some operations take longer than a client, a gateway or a load balancer will hold a connection open: a bulk export, a report, a provisioning step. HTTP has a status code for the case. RFC 9110 defines 202 Accepted as accepted for processing but not completed, and calls it intentionally noncommittal: the request may still be refused when the processing runs, and HTTP has no way to deliver a status code later. The 202 therefore has to carry a pointer to where the outcome will appear.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as API
  participant W as Worker
  C->>A: POST /exports
  A->>W: enqueue job
  A-->>C: 202 Accepted with operation id
  C->>A: GET /operations/id
  A-->>C: 200 done false
  W-->>A: result stored
  C->>A: GET /operations/id
  A-->>C: 200 done true with result link
blocks.legend: The long-running operation pattern: the API accepts the job, returns an operation resource, and the client polls it until done is true. The 202 and the status resource follow RFC 9110 and the Azure guidance (s2, s5).

blocks.text: The Azure guidance spells out the mechanics. The asynchronous method returns 202 with the status endpoint's URI in the Location header. A GET on that endpoint returns the current status, optionally an estimated completion time and a link to cancel. When the operation creates a resource, the status endpoint answers 303 See Other with the new resource's URI in Location once it is done, so a client following redirects lands on the result. In Google's APIs the same pattern is a single Operation resource type shared by every API, with a done flag, a metadata message for progress and either a response or an error on completion.

Polling needs a cadence the server controls. Return Retry-After on the status resource, and treat a client that ignores it like any other caller over its limit. Operation resources are garbage: give them an expiry, and document it. For events the server originates, such as a job finishing or a payment settling, the inverse pattern is a webhook: the consumer registers an endpoint, the API posts to it, and because delivery is at least once the payload carries an event id for deduplication and a signature so the receiver can verify the sender. The design question is the same as for the 202: what the client does when it never hears back.

Decide the threshold once, as a number of seconds, and make every operation that can exceed it asynchronous from the start. Converting a synchronous call to a 202 later is a breaking change for every client that expected the body.

subtopics.title: What counts as breaking, and how to version

blocks.text: Google's compatibility guidance separates three kinds of compatibility. Source compatibility means code written against the old version still compiles with the new client library; wire compatibility means it still talks to the new server; semantic compatibility means it still receives what a reasonable developer would expect. The last is the hardest, because clients depend on undocumented behaviour, and the guidance treats a visible behaviour change as breaking whenever reasonable user code would break.

blocks.caption: Which changes are compatible within a major version, from AIP-180. Default behaviour is part of the contract: a new default page size or sort order breaks clients even though the schema is unchanged.
rows: add a method, a resource or an optional field
old clients ignore what they do not know; a new field defaults to the old behaviour
add an enum value in a response
generated clients may reject an unknown value; document that the enum grows
a rename is a remove plus an add; add the new, keep the old
even a wire-compatible change alters the generated code
change the set of valid resource names
users store and validate names; breaks across major versions too
change a default, a limit or an ordering
a semantic change that reasonable code depends on

blocks.text: Every incompatible change needs a mechanism, and there are four: a version in the path, in a query parameter, in a header, or negotiated through the media type. The Azure guidance lists their trade-offs: path versioning is the simplest to route and cache but puts the version into every link; query and header versions keep one URI per resource; media type versioning fits content negotiation but is the least visible. Zalando's guidelines take a position: avoid versioning by preferring compatible extensions, and when it is unavoidable use media type versioning, never a version in the URL.

Stripe took a third path. Its versions are rolling and named by release date, each carrying a small set of incompatible changes so that upgrades stay incremental. An account is pinned to the current version at its first request until its owner upgrades, and a header overrides the pin per request. Each incompatible change is a version change module that transforms the current response backwards, applied in order until the caller's version is reached, so old versions stay out of the core code and the changelog is generated from the modules. The post reports almost a hundred such upgrades over six years without a major version.

blocks.title: The parallel change (expand and contract) for a rename, which the compatibility rules turn from a break into three releases.
items: Expand: add the new field or method beside the old one and populate both; the old clients notice nothing.
Migrate: move every client to the new field, one at a time; for external clients this is the longest phase, bounded by a published deprecation window.
Contract: once usage of the old field is zero on the metrics, remove it and the code that filled it.

subtopics.title: Contracts: OpenAPI, protobuf and generated clients

blocks.text: A contract is the API written down in a form a machine can check. For HTTP APIs the form is an OpenAPI description, whose current version is 3.2.1. Its Paths Object holds the relative path of every endpoint and the operations on it; each operation declares its parameters, request body and the responses by status code; and the Components Object holds the reusable schemas, parameters, responses and security schemes that the operations reference, so that the error shape or the pagination parameters are defined once. The same file drives documentation, client and server generation, mock servers and request validation.

For RPC between services the contract is usually a protobuf service definition, and gRPC generates the client and server stubs from it. A gRPC service defines four kinds of method: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming, and the framework guarantees message order within one call. Deadlines are part of the contract: a client states how long it will wait, and the server can check how much time remains before starting expensive work. The schema is binary and versioned by field number, which is what makes add-a-field compatible on the wire.

blocks.caption: What a contract gives each party, and the house rules that keep it true.

review the description in the pull request, before the handlers
request validation, conformance tests, a diff that flags breaking changes in continuous integration
one authoritative description in source control; the running service is tested against it
routing, authentication and quota configuration, per-version metrics
operations are tagged and named; large descriptions are split by reference

blocks.text: Design first or code first is a choice of where the single source of truth lives, not of whether to have one. Generating the description from code exposes whatever the framework produced and makes the review happen after the fact; writing it first lets consumers comment on names, errors and pagination while the service is still a stub. Either way the file is linted against the house style and diffed on every change, and a change that the diff classes as breaking against the compatibility table fails the build unless it comes with a new version.
The contract is the deliverable of API design. If a decision about paths, errors, pagination or versions is not in the description, it has not been made.

subtopics.title: REST, gRPC or GraphQL: choosing per boundary

blocks.text: The three styles answer different questions, and a system usually carries more than one. A public API over HTTP and JSON is readable with any tool, cacheable by any intermediary and the easiest to document and support for years. gRPC gives internal services a typed binary contract, streaming in both directions and deadlines built in, at the cost of needing a generated client and a proxy for browsers. GraphQL gives client teams a single endpoint and a query language, so a mobile screen fetches exactly its fields in one round trip instead of chaining several chatty REST calls.

GraphQL's flexibility has a server-side price that the project's own documentation names. A naive resolver per field turns one request for a list into N follow-up queries, the N+1 problem, which is solved by batching loads over a short window with a tool such as DataLoader. Because a client can ask for anything the schema allows, the server needs demand control: paginated list fields, limits on operation depth and breadth, and query complexity analysis. Queries are sent as POST by default, so HTTP caching needs the GET form or a client-side cache. These are solvable, but they are work that a REST API does not have.

blocks.caption: Picking the API style for one boundary of a design.

rows.pick_when: the consumers are external or unknown, the data is resource-shaped, intermediaries should cache reads, and the API will be supported for years with a deprecation policy
rows.avoid_when: the calls are streams or long-lived sessions, or the boundary is internal and chatty enough that per-call overhead dominates
rows.example: the public orders API of a shop; a partner integration

rows.pick_when: service to service inside one organisation, typed contracts and generated clients in several languages, streaming or deadlines matter
rows.avoid_when: browsers or third parties are the clients and no gateway translates for them; the team cannot maintain the schema discipline
rows.example: the fan-out and ranking calls behind a feed service

rows.pick_when: several client applications need different slices of a rich graph and the team owning the schema can batch, paginate and bound every query
rows.avoid_when: the API is public to unknown callers, or the data is flat and one REST resource per screen already fits
rows.example: a mobile app's backend-for-frontend over a dozen internal services

blocks.text: The usual layering is public REST at the edge, gRPC between services and, where the client teams need it, a GraphQL layer that composes the internal services for the user interface. Each boundary then has its own versioning policy and its own contract format, and the compatibility rules above apply to all three: a removed protobuf field or a removed GraphQL type breaks a client exactly as a removed JSON field does.

worked_example.title: Worked example: the orders API of a small shop, from resources to a contract

blocks.text: A shop needs an API for its own web and mobile clients and for a few partners. The design walks the lesson in order: resources, methods, pagination, a long-running export, the error shape and one compatible change. Every quantity below is an assumption stated so a reviewer can attack it; the only cited facts are the HTTP semantics and the pagination rules.

blocks.title: Designing the orders API
items: List the resources: customers, orders and order lines; the lines live under their order, so the deepest path is 3 segments (collection, item, collection) and nothing nests further.

Map the methods: a POST on the orders collection creates (201 with a Location header), a PATCH changes the shipping address, and cancellation is a custom method, POST on the order with the verb cancel, so that it can be refused with a 409 when the order has already shipped.
Pick the page size: a default of 25 orders per page, which is the Azure example value, and a hard cap of 100; a request for 500 is clamped to 100 and the contract says so.

Size the deep page problem: the largest partner has 12,000 orders, which is 120 pages at the cap; with offsets the last page skips 11,900 rows on every read, so the list uses an opaque cursor over the order id.

Find the slow operation: a full export of 12,000 orders with lines is measured at about 90 seconds against a gateway that closes idle connections after 30 seconds, so the export is a long-running operation.
Shape it: POST /exports returns 202 with the operation URI in Location; the operation resource answers with Retry-After of 10 seconds until done, then 303 to the file in object storage.
Define the error shape once: a Problem Details object with an errors extension listing field, reason and message; a 429 carries Retry-After; stack traces never appear.

Make one compatible change: the postal code field is renamed; expand adds postal_code beside zip and fills both, migrate runs for the 90-day deprecation window published in the contract, contract removes zip when its usage metric reads 0 for 2 weeks.
Write it down: the OpenAPI description below is the contract; it is reviewed in the pull request before the handlers, linted, and diffed on every change.
